lesson.title: How Badly Does an Atom Want One More Electron
lesson.summary: Electron affinity measures the energy change when a gaseous atom gains an extra electron, and unlike ionization energy, the most favorable values cluster among the nonmetals racing to complete their valence shells.
lesson.body:
Ionization energy asks how hard it is to take an electron away from an atom, electron affinity asks the opposite question: what happens energetically when an atom gains one. Formally, electron affinity is the energy change for the process X(g) plus an electron yields X-(g). For most nonmetals, adding an electron is favorable and releases energy, so the electron affinity is a negative number, reflecting an exothermic process. The more negative the value, the more strongly the atom attracts the incoming electron. This puts electron affinity in the same family of ideas as ionization energy and periodic trends: both describe how strongly a nucleus, filtered through its own valence electron configuration, competes for electrons.

Across a period, electron affinity generally becomes more negative moving left to right, mirroring the rise in effective nuclear charge that also drives ionization energy upward. Atoms on the right side of the periodic table are just one or two electrons short of a full valence shell, so pulling in one more electron moves them toward that stable, low energy noble gas configuration, and a lot of energy is released in the process. Carbon's electron affinity is about negative 122 kilojoules per mole, while fluorine's is about negative 328 kilojoules per mole, reflecting how close fluorine already sits to a filled shell.

The group 15 elements interrupt this trend for the same reason nitrogen interrupts the ionization energy trend. Nitrogen's 2p3 configuration is half filled and unusually stable, so forcing a fourth electron into that subshell is actually unfavorable: nitrogen's electron affinity is close to zero, and by some conventions slightly positive, meaning the process absorbs energy rather than releasing it. Oxygen, one element over, has a strongly negative electron affinity of about negative 141 kilojoules per mole, because its 2p4 configuration still has room to accept one more electron into an already occupied orbital without breaking a stable half filled arrangement.

Down a group, electron affinity generally becomes less negative, since the added electron lands farther from the nucleus in a larger orbital and is shielded by more core electrons. But the halogens hide a well known exception at the very top of the group. Fluorine's electron affinity, at negative 328 kilojoules per mole, is actually less negative than chlorine's, at negative 349 kilojoules per mole, even though fluorine sits higher and would be expected to hold the record. Fluorine's 2p subshell is so small and already so crowded with electrons that the incoming electron experiences significant repulsion from the electrons already there, which offsets some of the energy released by the strong nuclear attraction. Chlorine's larger 3p subshell has more room, so it accepts an extra electron more favorably despite its smaller effective nuclear charge.

Electron affinity also comes with a second, often overlooked warning: adding a second electron to an already negative ion is always unfavorable. Turning O- into O2- absorbs a large amount of energy, about positive 744 kilojoules per mole, because you are forcing a negative charge onto a particle that is already negatively charged and actively repels it. This matters later on, because it means ionic compounds containing multiply charged anions, like oxide or sulfide, only form because the energy released when the crystal lattice assembles more than makes up for that unfavorable second electron affinity step.
